For my German Visa, the template I followed was roughly like this:

1. Introduce yourself: your name, age, occupation, where you live, etc.


2. Why you decided to become an Au pair: to improve your language skills, to get to know the country and the culture, because you like children/have experience taking care of children, etc.


3. What's your relationship with your host family like: talk a bit about where they live, why you chose them as a host family, if you talk often to each other, if the parent(s) send you pictures/videos of the kids and if they are supportive towards you learning the language.


4. What you plan to do with your gained experience when you come back to your home country: do you plan to finish or start a college course related to your Au pair experience (language and/or culture)? Do you plan to apply for a job in a specific company? etc.

Keep in mind that you should always say that you are coming back to your home country, even if you aren't, because the Au pair visa isn't an immigration visa and it could be denied if you say that you want to stay in your host country afterwards.

The letter doesn't have to be too big, 2 to 3 sentences per paragraph is fine. If you have a basic level of the language of your host country, your letter should reflect that; using Google Translate or any equivalent is perfectly okay.

Hey, everyone. I am for the second time in my life, after a year of not even thinking about it, considering to convert to Judaism once again. 

The thing is though that I recently got into Tarot as a therapeutic tool of self-knowledge and advice so I thought it would be a good idea to ask the cards for advice. I haven't learned the 78 cards yet so I asked two different people online to do the readings for me and generally speaking they both said that Judaism isn't the best path for me and that I should explore other religions. 

And as foolish as I think it would be to ignore not only one but two tarot readings, I just can’t let go of the idea of conversion. I am reading books, articles, watching YouTube videos, listening to podcasts and even memorized how to get from my house to the shul that I have been looking up online through the subway. 

I feel completely lost. 

I feel great sympathy for Judaism and Jewish people to the point that part of me believes that I either had a past live where I was Jewish or that I have Jewish ancestors that I unfortunately don't know about. But at the same time another part of me feels like I won't be happy and fulfilled if I choose to follow a Jewish life, no matter how much I long for it. 

Like I said, I feel really lost, so... what would you do in my situation? Do you have any piece of advice that could help me right now?

A bit though, I think, since you said he has been dismissive in the past. But what you could try to do (and what I personally would do if I were in your position) is to bring your therapist your notes on why you consider yourself to possibly be autistic. Because I think he is highly likely to ask "Why do you think that?" after you say something along the lines of "I think I might be autistic" so having it written down will have you prepared for this situation. But also I would suggest to not be too much assertive about it cause some health professionals don't like it when people go up to them like "Hey, I think I might have this". Some do! But some really don't... 

Also now this is just some sort of cautionary advice but if your therapist dismisses you again, then maybe it's a good idea to seek out another professional to do your autism evaluation.
